claim: MTD tests mostly run against attacker models far simpler than an APT
quote: The most glaring flaw in the MTD literature is the ill-defined attacker models [ 7], which are often too simplistic or based on completely unrealistic assumptions. ... Furthermore, testing against active scanning (Nmap [ 52]) is too naive. Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time.
issue: Jalowski says attacker models are 'often' too simplistic, not that 'most' tests use them; the simplicity finding is credited to their 2022 survey [7]; the 'run in simulation' clause is not in Jalowski and must rest on cho2020.

claim: Each evaluation chooses its own metrics, so MTD mechanisms cannot be compared across evaluations
quote: Instead, many authors propose their own idea on how to test the effectiveness of MTD strategies, using their own metrics and frameworks ... While these individual approaches are not necessarily incorrect, the lack of a universal metric prevents any objective cross-technique comparison, leaving a critical gap in the holistic evaluation of MTD efficacy.
locator: p. 2 printed (PDF p. 2), Sec. 1.1; p. 5 printed (PDF p. 5), Sec. 3.1
issue: Source says 'many authors' (and 'predominantly', Sec. 3.1) use their own metrics, not each evaluation; the comparison consequence is supported.
fix_text: 'Each evaluation chooses its own, so' -> 'Evaluations choose their own, so'

claim: jalowski2026 is a survey of MTD that finds MTD attacker models lack properties of an APT attacker
quote: The presented paper moves from “survey and taxonomy” found in the prior literature to gap analysis and actionable research directions. ... The most glaring flaw in the MTD literature is the ill-defined attacker models [ 7], which are often too simplistic or based on completely unrealistic assumptions. ... Furthermore, testing against active scanning (Nmap [ 52]) is too naive. Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time.
locator: p. 3 printed (PDF p. 3), Sec. 1.2; p. 8 printed (PDF p. 8), Sec. 4.3
issue: The substance holds, but the paper calls itself a gap analysis that moves beyond survey, and credits the attacker-model flaw to its authors' 2022 survey [7] (Jalowski, Zmuda, Rawski, Electronics 2022). Same 'survey' label in U0231, U0299, U0841.
fix_text: 'Two surveys of MTD find' -> 'A survey and a gap analysis of MTD find' (or keep 'surveys' as Marc's ruling)

claim: Jalowski contributes learning and deployment-strategy awareness to the four properties the surveys add
quote: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time. To move forward, research must shift toward defending against smart, adaptive attackers [6] who understand the MTD scheme and look for the mathematical logic behind the movement.
issue: Jalowski carries learning and deployment-strategy awareness only; choice of attack strategy and cost-benefit reasoning must rest on cho2020. 'Surveys' label: see U0226.

claim: Jalowski et al. call the attacker model 'the most glaring flaw in the MTD literature' (p. 8)
quote: The most glaring flaw in the MTD literature is the ill-defined attacker models [ 7], which are often too simplistic or based on completely unrealistic assumptions.
issue: Quote and pinpoint are exact, but the flaw named is the 'ill-defined attacker models', not the attacker model as such; the sentence drops 'ill-defined'.
fix_text: 'call the attacker model' -> 'call ill-defined attacker models'

claim: Jalowski finds the same lack of learning and deployment-strategy awareness as Cho (first half of the sentence U0239 completes)
quote: To move forward, research must shift toward defending against smart, adaptive attackers [6] who understand the MTD scheme and look for the mathematical logic behind the movement.
issue: Uncited fragment; the inventory split one sentence into U0238 and U0239. Carried by the citation at the end of U0239.

claim: An APT attacker learns the MTD's deployment patterns over time and looks for the logic of the deployment strategy
quote: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time. To move forward, research must shift toward defending against smart, adaptive attackers [6] who understand the MTD scheme and look for the mathematical logic behind the movement.
issue: Learning mutation patterns is said of APTs; looking for the logic of the movement is said of 'smart, adaptive attackers [6]' (a cite to Cho), not of APTs. The sentence merges the two subjects.

claim: MTD is typically tested against active scanning such as Nmap, while an APT attacker uses passive reconnaissance to stay hidden
quote: Furthermore, testing against active scanning (Nmap [ 52]) is too naive. Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows ... To make matters worse, it is commonly calculated using simple Nmap scans [52] as a baseline
locator: p. 8 printed (PDF p. 8), Sec. 4.3; p. 9 printed (PDF p. 9), Sec. 5
issue: 'Typically' rests on p. 9, where 'commonly' is said of how ASP is calculated, not of MTD testing in general; close enough, but the strongest reading of 'typically' is the session's.

claim: Detection avoidance includes choosing techniques an IDS does not flag, such as passive reconnaissance (Jalowski's share of row 5)
quote: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows
issue: Jalowski carries the passive-reconnaissance example and staying hidden; the IDS framing and 'low and slow' are not Jalowski's (low and slow rests on alshamrani2019).

claim: Learning: keeps the patterns it observes in past MTD deployments and uses them to choose later techniques (Jalowski's share of row 7)
quote: utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time.
issue: Jalowski carries learning patterns over time; 'uses them to choose later techniques' is not in Jalowski and must rest on cho2020.

claim: Deployment-strategy awareness: predicts and leverages which mechanism the deployment strategy deploys next, and when (Jalowski's share of row 8)
quote: To move forward, research must shift toward defending against smart, adaptive attackers [6] who understand the MTD scheme and look for the mathematical logic behind the movement. ... If any mathematical correlation exists between MTD states, a skilled attacker can predict future movements or decipher past communications.
locator: p. 8 printed (PDF p. 8), Sec. 4.3; p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7), Sec. 4.1
issue: Jalowski's attacker predicts the next state of a moving parameter (the 'movement'), not which mechanism is deployed next; the 'which mechanism' reading must come from cho2020 or is ours.

claim: Jalowski finds that MTD attacker models lack properties of an APT attacker
quote: The most glaring flaw in the MTD literature is the ill-defined attacker models [ 7], which are often too simplistic or based on completely unrealistic assumptions. ... Furthermore, testing against active scanning (Nmap [ 52]) is too naive. Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time.
issue: As U0226: substance holds; 'survey' label and the attacker-model finding credited to the authors' 2022 survey [7]. Provenance from-memory, but the claim survives.

claim: MTD mechanisms cannot be compared across evaluations because each evaluation chooses its own metrics
quote: Instead, many authors propose their own idea on how to test the effectiveness of MTD strategies, using their own metrics and frameworks ... While these individual approaches are not necessarily incorrect, the lack of a universal metric prevents any objective cross-technique comparison, leaving a critical gap in the holistic evaluation of MTD efficacy.
locator: p. 2 printed (PDF p. 2), Sec. 1.1; p. 5 printed (PDF p. 5), Sec. 3.1
issue: As U0210: 'many authors', not each evaluation. The p. 2 statement itself attributes the comparison gap to 'recent surveys [5-7]'.
fix_text: 'because each evaluation chooses its own metrics' -> 'because evaluations choose their own metrics'

claim: That MTD attacker models in general lack the properties of an APT attacker is Jalowski's finding
quote: The most glaring flaw in the MTD literature is the ill-defined attacker models [ 7], which are often too simplistic or based on completely unrealistic assumptions. ... Furthermore, testing against active scanning (Nmap [ 52]) is too naive. Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time.
issue: 'The properties' (definite) reads as the eight of Table 3.2; Jalowski names only passive reconnaissance, learning and scheme awareness, and says 'often', not 'in general'. 'Survey' label: see U0226.
fix_text: 'lack the properties of an APT attacker' -> 'lack properties of an APT attacker'
